blogs.title: After Ciminelli, Fraudulent-Inducement Finds Its Footing in §1348
blogs.description: The Fifth Circuit draws a bright line between the Supreme Court’s rejection of the right-to-control theory in Ciminelli and the acceptance of fraudulent-inducement in Kousisis, and plants §1348 squarely on the latter ground. By framing the pump‑and‑dump allegations as lies that induced investors to part with their money, the panel treats the property interest as cash, not mere “valuable economic information.” The post unpacks how Constantinescu operationalizes Kousisis for securities fraud, why post-Ciminelli motions framing misstatements as informational deprivations will falter, and how this aligns with emerging circuit practice (including the Seventh Circuit’s Smith).

blogs.title: Profit Motive as Fraud Intent: Constantinescu’s Mens Rea Lesson for Pump-and-Dumps
blogs.description: Relying on Kousisis, the Fifth Circuit rejects the argument that intent to profit is incompatible with intent to defraud because victims received market‑value shares. The post explains why fraud does not require intending net economic harm, how “money in mind” suffices where defendants seek to obtain cash by deceit, and what kinds of evidence will matter at trial (timing of trades, misstatements about positions, and inducement). It also flags the limits of defenses premised on disclaimers or generalized market risk when concrete misrepresentations are alleged.

blogs.title: Finfluencers, Beware: Constantinescu Signals Criminal Exposure for Social-Media Touting
blogs.description: This decision underscores that influencer hype crosses into criminal territory when false statements about positions or price targets are used to induce trades. The post situates §1348 alongside Rule 10b‑5 and SEC Section 17(b) touting cases, highlights the risks around undisclosed conflicts and misrepresented holdings, and explains why “not financial advice” disclaimers won’t insulate deliberate deception. It offers practical compliance takeaways for creators, funds partnering with influencers, and platforms hosting finance content in light of DOJ’s willingness to charge social‑media manipulation as securities fraud.

blogs.title: Charging Choices and Pleading Standards: Why §1348 Indictments Will Survive Motions to Dismiss
blogs.description: Constantinescu is a primer on indictment sufficiency under §1348: track the statutory elements, allege a deceptive scheme and an object of obtaining money, and dismissal is unlikely. The post examines the court’s reliance on mail/wire‑fraud concepts (via Greenlaw), the rejection of early merits fights masquerading as property‑interest challenges, and the strategic appeal of §1348 over more intricate Title 15 theories. It closes with what defense counsel can still press pretrial (particularity, materiality, and scienter disputes) and what must await the jury.
